explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jeremiah, the prophet telling this story, says the LORD showed him "two baskets of figs placed in front of the temple of the LORD." (Jeremiah 24:1) Not a pot, not a branch, just two baskets of fruit sitting right there. I've baked a lot of batches and I've never once had a vision about them, so I'm a little jealous.

A boiling pot is something Jeremiah sees, but in a different passage (Jeremiah 1:13). Here the LORD shows him "two baskets of figs placed in front of the temple of the LORD." (Jeremiah 24:1) Baskets, not a pot. Easy to mix up when your head is in the kitchen, and mine is always in the kitchen.

explanations.answer: A branch from an almond tree
explanations.explanation: An almond branch is something Jeremiah sees too, but that's in Jeremiah 1:11. This time the LORD shows him "two baskets of figs placed in front of the temple of the LORD." (Jeremiah 24:1) So the picture here is fruit in baskets. Same prophet, different vision.

Not quite, baker. The text says the other basket held "very poor figs, so bad they could not be eaten." (Jeremiah 24:2) That's not a little rough. That's a basket nobody is touching. If I served a batch like that, even the crumbs would file a complaint.

Right. The other basket held "very poor figs, so bad they could not be eaten." (Jeremiah 24:2) Nobody was going to nibble on those and say they weren't so bad. The text leaves no wiggle room, and neither do I.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, "Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah…" (Jeremiah 24:5) These are the people Babylon carried away. You'd expect the ones who got hauled off to be the bad basket, right? The LORD flips that around.

Close, but it's the other way around. The people left in Jerusalem fall with the bad figs, because the LORD says, "But like the bad figs, so bad they cannot be eaten… so will I deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the remnant of Jerusalem…" (Jeremiah 24:8) Zedekiah is the king of Judah in this part. The good figs are the exiles, the ones who were sent away. It's a surprise, and I'd have guessed wrong too.

The priests don't show up in this comparison at all. The LORD says, "Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah…" (Jeremiah 24:5) The baskets sat in front of the temple, but the good figs are the exiles. Don't let the location fool you, friend.

True. The LORD says the exiles are those "whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans." (Jeremiah 24:5) Chaldeans is another name for the people of Babylon. He says it plainly, and He's still calling these exiles good.

It's actually true. The LORD says the exiles are those "whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans." (Jeremiah 24:5) The Chaldeans are the people of Babylon. He names Himself as the One who sent them, and right in the same breath He calls them good.
Yes, baker. God says, "I will build them up and not tear them down…" (Jeremiah 24:6) Building up is the opposite of tearing down, and He says both out loud. This one's going in the box.
That's right. God says, "…I will plant them and not uproot them." (Jeremiah 24:6) Planting and not uprooting go together, like a seed that gets to stay in the ground. Good eye, friend.

Wash is a fine word, but it's not in this verse. God says, "I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them." (Jeremiah 24:6) Build and plant are the two words He uses. Washing is for dishes, and trust me, I've done plenty of those.

Call doesn't fit here. The verse says, "I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them." (Jeremiah 24:6) Both blanks are words of putting something up and keeping it in place. No phone calls in this one, friend.

Seal is a word I love, because I seal cookie boxes all day, but it's not in this verse. God says, "I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them." (Jeremiah 24:6) The words are build and plant. Save the sealing for the boxes.

explanations.answer: They will turn back to Him completely
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. God says, "They will be My people, and I will be their God, for they will return to Me with all their heart." (Jeremiah 24:7) The reason is right there in the verse: they come back with all their heart. Not half, not most of the way. All of it.

explanations.answer: They will offer Him sacrifices in Babylon
explanations.explanation: Sacrifices aren't the reason God gives. He says, "They will be My people, and I will be their God, for they will return to Me with all their heart." (Jeremiah 24:7) The reason is their return with all their heart. Nothing about sacrifices shows up in this verse.

explanations.answer: They will fight for Him against Babylon
explanations.explanation: No fighting in this verse, friend. God says, "They will be My people, and I will be their God, for they will return to Me with all their heart." (Jeremiah 24:7) The reason is that they return to Him with all their heart. Nobody picks up a sword here.

You got it, baker. God says He'll deal with "Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the remnant of Jerusalem—those remaining in this land and those living in the land of Egypt." (Jeremiah 24:8) So the bad basket reaches past the borders. Some had gone down to Egypt, and they're counted too.

Moab isn't named here. The verse says, "…the remnant of Jerusalem—those remaining in this land and those living in the land of Egypt." (Jeremiah 24:8) Egypt is the place on the list. Moab never makes it into this verse.

Assyria doesn't make the list. The verse says, "…the remnant of Jerusalem—those remaining in this land and those living in the land of Egypt." (Jeremiah 24:8) The answer is Egypt. Easy one to miss when you're counting empires.

Right, baker. God says He'll make them "a disgrace and an object of scorn, ridicule, and cursing wherever I have banished them." (Jeremiah 24:9) It's a heavy line, and I won't joke about it. Scorn is the word, and you caught it.

Honor is the opposite of what the verse says. God says He'll make them "a disgrace and an object of scorn, ridicule, and cursing wherever I have banished them." (Jeremiah 24:9) The word is scorn. It's a hard verse, friend, so no shame in flinching.

Praise points the wrong way here. The verse says, "a disgrace and an object of scorn, ridicule, and cursing wherever I have banished them." (Jeremiah 24:9) The word is scorn. This is a heavy part of the passage, friend.

True, baker. God says, "And I will send against them sword and famine and plague, until they have perished from the land that I gave to them and their fathers." (Jeremiah 24:10) It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to sit quiet with it for a second. You read it right.

This one is true, friend. God says, "And I will send against them sword and famine and plague, until they have perished from the land that I gave to them and their fathers." (Jeremiah 24:10) It's a hard verse, and I think it hurts to read. The statement matches the text.
